title: What is Learning?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: A short intellectual history of what the word 'learning' has been taken to mean, ending in a working definition a teacher can act on. Hendrick sets Plato's anamnesis - learning as recollection of truths the soul already holds - against Locke's blank slate, and dismisses both before moving to the modern era. He then uses Richard Mayer's three dominant metaphors (response strengthening, information acquisition, knowledge construction) as the twentieth-century map, adding evolutionary psychology's claim that some learning capacities are evolved adaptations rather than general-purpose processes. The pivot of the piece is his own preference: thinking of the brain as a limited-resource system with real constraints on attention, processing and encoding, because that is the view that disciplines instructional design. He also handles salience carefully, noting that emotionally charged experience produces durable memory traces but is a poor model for learning to drive or solve quadratics. He lands on Kirschner's definition - learning as a change in long-term memory - defending it not as the most beautiful account but as the most honest and the most actionable for teachers and parents.
points: Hendrick's verdict on Plato and Locke is that both were wrong yet both dominated the field for centuries, which is his warning about how long attractive metaphors of learning outlive their evidence.

Mayer's three metaphors are presented as a diagnostic for a teacher's own implicit theory: response strengthening handles habit, information acquisition mistakes exposure for retention, knowledge construction alone treats learning as active organisation.

The limited-resource framing of the brain is offered as the single most useful lens for instructional design, because attention, processing and encoding constraints are what determine whether a lesson design can work at all.

The salience point cuts against an obvious inference: flashbulb memories show emotion strengthens memory traces, but emotionally charged events are not a usable mechanism for teaching driving or quadratic equations.
Hendrick defends 'a change in long-term memory' on pragmatic grounds - it is the definition that gives teachers and parents something they can actually influence.
quotes: For Plato, learning was not an acquisition but a recollection; a remembering of truths the soul has always known which he termed anamnesis. In his dialogue "Meno," Plato demonstrates this through Socrates' interaction with an uneducated slave boy who, without formal instruction, successfully solves a geometric problem through carefully guided questioning.

Of course both of them were wrong, but their ideas would dominate conceptions of learning right up until the relatively recent past. Over the last 100 years, three paradigms of learning have taken root.

Learning as Response Strengthening – Rooted in behaviourism, this view sees learning as a process of reinforcing correct responses. While useful for habit formation, it oversimplifies the complexity of understanding and application.

Evolutionary psychology adds another dimension, suggesting that certain learning capacities represent adaptations shaped by natural selection. Our propensity for language acquisition, face recognition, and threat detection reflect specialised learning mechanisms that evolved to solve recurring problems in our ancestral environment.

But learning is also about a particular kind of focus. “Learning is a matter of intensity, not elapsed time” said Robert Heinlein and this is certainly true in terms of what neuroscientists call "salience"; the quality that makes some stimuli stand out from others. Emotionally charged, personally relevant, or deeply engaging learning experiences receive preferential processing in the brain, creating memory traces resistant to decay.

Paul defined learning as a change in long term memory and I think it’s my favourite definition because it’s the one that helped me most as a teacher when I heard it first. It may not have Platonic mysticism or Lockean optimism, but it’s the most honest, and it affords a particular kind of hope for teachers and parents because we can do something about it.
